papers.title: Shallow may be better: Physics-Constrained Lightweight Networks for High-Throughput Particle Image Velocimetry
papers.abstract: Convolutional networks for optical flow typically adopt progressively deeper pyramidal encoders under the assumption that larger receptive fields improve motion estimation. For particle image velocimetry (PIV), however, tracer-particle displacement between frames is bounded by the acquisition geometry, allowing network depth to be derived from the physically admissible displacement rather than inherited from general-purpose architectures. Using a layer-by-layer analysis of spatial-support growth, we derive its explicit upper bound and show that deeper architectures substantially exceed the support required for PIV, compromising training stability, spatial resolution under particle loss, and inference efficiency. Based on this analysis, we develop LIMA3, a lightweight pyramidal displacement estimator with 589,000 trainable parameters. Across synthetic and experimental benchmarks, LIMA3 matches the accuracy of established learned and classical methods with at least an order of magnitude less memory and substantially higher throughput, while retaining the physically expected coarsening of spatial resolution as tracer information is lost. Its linear memory scaling enables megapixel processing within embedded memory budgets, such that LIMA3 can reach over 900 image pairs per second at $640\times480$~pixel on an RTX 5090 and 99 image pairs per second on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin. The spatial-support analysis provides a transferable design principle for compact optical-flow architectures and bounded-window attention, offering an alternative to compressing oversized general-purpose networks and enabling efficient operation alongside image acquisition.

papers.title: ISLA: A Coordinate-Free, Measure-Weighted Transformer for Boundary-Driven PDEs
papers.abstract: Symmetry is a foundational principle of physics: the behavior of a PDE-governed system does not depend on the coordinate frame, unit system, or mesh used to write it down, and neither should a surrogate model. Yet today's leading neural surrogates lack these invariances and fail under simple transformations of the same problem: for models trained on PDEs of cars in one pose (i.e., translation and rotation), rotating the full PDE raises the surface-pressure error from 4% to more than 100%, and re-sampling its boundary raises it to about 30%. We introduce ISLA (Invariant Slice Attention), a slice-attention transformer for steady, boundary-driven PDEs. Because the boundary determines the interior solution, ISLA encodes the posed boundary once into learned slices and evaluates arbitrary interior points independently through a tree-accelerated learned boundary kernel. Inputs are nondimensionalized in scales computed from the boundary, sums over boundary cells are area-weighted quadratures that converge under mesh refinement, and geometry enters only as distances and relative angles to equivariant slice anchors, making the model equivariant to rigid motions and reflections up to optional token subsampling and tree clustering. On AeroZoo, 2,816 3D flows spanning diverse geometries, poses, physical scales, and boundary conditions, ISLA's mean reference-scaled velocity and pressure errors are 1.9 and 2.2 times lower than the best baseline's. On full AirfRANS, ISLA is second only to an explicit boundary-integral network (GLOBE), with errors 1.6 to 2.6 times lower than the better of Transolver's and GeoTransolver's in every field.

papers.title: AeroZoo: A Benchmark of Well-Posed Flow Problems for Foundation Models of Aerodynamics
papers.abstract: Neural surrogates for computational fluid dynamics (CFD) are trained and ranked on single-family, fixed-domain datasets that cannot test the minimum bar for an aerodynamic foundation model: predicting CFD-quality incompressible flow in seconds for new shapes in new enclosures. On DrivAerML, larger models and longer training barely lower Transolver's error; doubling training cases cuts it by about 12% up to 400 cases, exhausting the dataset. We introduce AeroZoo, a benchmark and training corpus of 3,815 time-mean unsteady Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (URANS) solutions with a transition model across seven geometry families, eight enclosures, and Reynolds numbers from $10^3$ to $10^8$. Each sample poses a well-posed PDE problem as a solver receives it: boundary meshes grouped by condition type, prescribed values, and fluid properties. The 2,816 time-mean-stable samples form the canonical benchmark: two tasks, mean engineering metrics with an overall flow score $S_{\mathrm{flow}}$ (1.000 for uniform inlet flow), and 22 frozen geometry-disjoint splits holding out shapes, enclosures, boundary-condition layouts, and Reynolds ranges. On the random split, boundary-condition tokens cut GeoTransolver's mean velocity error from 89.8% to 15.2% of inlet speed (uniform flow: 44.0%; $S_{\mathrm{flow}} = 0.290$). ISLA, a boundary-driven transformer, reaches 8.2% ($S_{\mathrm{flow}} = 0.153$; 0.123 with boundary targets), about 6 times mesh-refinement sensitivity. On shared test samples, holding out a geometry family barely changes ISLA's mean velocity error, whereas holding out enclosures or boundary-condition layouts raises it 3.8 to 8.4 times. The dataset is public; the scoring code will be released.

papers.title: Failure Modes and Data-Efficient Remedies for Transformer-Based Prediction of Viscoplastic Flows
papers.abstract: Fast and accurate prediction of viscoplastic flows remains a challenge in computational rheology due to yield surfaces, discontinuous gradients, and strongly nonlinear transitions between yielded and unyielded regions. Transformer-based neural operators such as RheOFormer have recently shown strong potential for surrogate modeling of non-Newtonian flows. However, their applicability to viscoplastic systems and their efficacy in recovering realistic flows remain poorly understood. In this work, we present the first systematic investigation of RheOFormer applied to steady Bingham channel flow. By isolating the problem to a simple geometry and constitutive model, we examine how dataset structure, numerical value range, and input representation govern the model's ability to interpolate and extrapolate within the parameter space. The data regimes in which RheOFormer remains accurate and those in which errors emerge are identified, particularly for plug-dominated flows and for conditions outside the velocity scales or flow structures represented during training. Upon identifying these failure modes, targeted enhancements to the input representation and loss formulation are introduced to better predict low-gradient plug regions. Logarithmic velocity representations and gradient-aware loss formulations substantially improve accuracy in challenging regimes where the baseline formulation fails. In addition, extrapolation errors are reduced by augmenting the training set with only a few strategically selected cases spanning the missing physical regimes. Finally, a single partially developed snapshot suffices for an accurate steady-state prediction, and the model outperforms simply copying its input throughout flow development. These results highlight the importance of appropriate field representation and parameter-space coverage for data-efficient neural-operator prediction of viscoplastic flows.

papers.title: A shock-fitting approach to high-order simulation of viscous hypersonic flows based on inviscid implicit shock tracking
papers.abstract: This work presents a framework for computing viscous, shock-dominated flows at high Mach and Reynolds numbers in which the bow shock is located by inviscid implicit shock tracking and then treated as a boundary of the viscous computation. The high-order implicit shock tracking (HOIST) method is applied to the Euler equations on a coarse, shock-agnostic mesh to produce a shock-aligned mesh and the shock geometry; the elements upstream of the shock are discarded, the post-shock domain is remeshed to resolve the boundary layer, and the compressible Navier-Stokes equations are solved on it with a high-order interior penalty discontinuous Galerkin method, with the post-shock state prescribed along the shock boundary by the oblique shock relations. Because the shock structure is never resolved, the approach requires neither the extreme element compression nor the specialized formulations that fully coupled viscous shock tracking demands at these conditions; the tracking optimization is confined to the coarse inviscid mesh, and the viscous computation involves no mesh unknowns and no additional nonlinear stabilization. The framework is demonstrated on a Mach 10.6 axisymmetric blunt cone, a Mach 17.6 cylinder, and a Mach 5 sphere in three dimensions, with surface pressure and heat flux in good agreement with experimental measurements and reference computations.

papers.title: Topological analysis of permeability tensor in anisotropic porous media
papers.abstract: The permeability of an anisotropic porous medium is a tensor whose off-diagonal components, which describe the deflection of the macroscopic flux away from the driving force, are small and change sign under reflections. We ask whether direction-aware topological data analysis can predict the full permeability tensor of three-dimensional porous media directly from their geometry. We introduce two direction-aware topological descriptors for flow problems: a cone-based filtration, adapted from our earlier work on the elastic stiffness tensor, and a throat-scale filtration built on the distance transform of the pore space. Using permeability tensors computed with the lattice Boltzmann method, we compare them with a comprehensive set of non-topological baselines, comprising statistical microstructure descriptors and physics-based permeability estimators. The topological descriptors are most informative for the off-diagonal components, which the baselines capture least well. There the throat-scale filtration alone outperforms every non-topological descriptor set, including the union of all statistical descriptors and physics-based estimators, and adding it to the baselines consistently improves the prediction. We also confirm the approach on real rock data.

papers.title: Cyclic changes of frame for designing non-retracing verification cases for numerical interface tracking
papers.abstract: A forward-backward deformation test supplies an exact final interface, but retracing can allow errors from the two halves to cancel. We construct alternative tests by superposing a cyclic change of frame on the same base deformation. The frame returns to its starting pose, preserving the exact final phase and the deformation history up to rigid placement. A small returning translation can keep trajectories close to the retraced ones. A full rotation about a fixed centre or axis gives closed paths with nonzero winding for material labels that stay off that centre or axis. For incompressible base fields the transformed velocity is divergence-free. We construct discretely solenoidal face fluxes for geometric volume-of-fluid advection by circulating the transformed potential. In three TwoPhaseFlow benchmarks, with a shared time grid for each pair, a full-turn frame increased the final cell-average shape discrepancy in all 30 comparisons, with a median factor of 1.50. The fitted convergence exponent decreased in each of the six benchmark-reconstruction comparisons over the tested grids.

papers.title: Flood forecasting using a physics-guided conditional denoising diffusion probabilistic model
papers.abstract: High-resolution flood forecasting with full two-dimensional shallow water equation (SWE) solvers remains computationally expensive, even on GPUs. We develop a conditional denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) that forecasts the evolution of 30 m water-depth fields over a four-day horizon for the Des Plaines River watershed, Illinois. The model is trained on SynxFlow SWE simulations of 113 historical storms observed across twelve Midwestern states (2003-2024), each under three antecedent-wetness scenarios, and can optionally be conditioned on coarse 100 m or 150 m hydrodynamic simulations. Because reverse diffusion is stochastic, every forecast is a 20-member ensemble drawn from the same trained model. Coarse conditioning reduces the four-day mean water-depth RMSE of the ensemble mean from 0.170 m to 0.054 m (100 m) and 0.048 m (150 m). The coarser 150 m conditioning also gives the best critical success index (0.839), false alarm ratio, CRPS and Brier score at lower cost, so finer conditioning does not guarantee better skill. Averaging members reduces error by 5-11% relative to a single realization, and the ensemble provides spatially explicit exceedance probabilities, although the ensembles are under-dispersive (spread-to-error ratios 0.35-0.73). On a single GPU, a four-day forecast over 26 non-overlapping patches is 7.8x, 11.0x and 16.3x faster than the 30 m simulation for the 100 m, 150 m and unconditioned configurations, and projected speedups for a 14-day forecast reach 12-49x for one member and 48-58x for 20 members. Physics-guided diffusion models are thus promising probabilistic surrogates for regional-scale flood forecasting.

papers.title: Deep Learning of Solver-Aware Turbulence Closures from Nudged LES Dynamics
papers.abstract: The differentiable physics paradigm may be leveraged as an a-posteriori approach for discovering turbulence closure models by embedding a neural network parameterization directly inside the solver and optimizing it given potentially sparse target data. This addresses a key limitation of a-priori learning where direct numerical simulation (DNS) data is used to approximate the subgrid stress with the assumption of a low-pass filter. Closures trained in this a-priori manner frequently lead to unstable deployments due to the mismatch between the assumed filter and the effect of numerical discretizations and coarse-graining. In comparison, while typically stable during deployment, a-posteriori learning incurs high computational costs due to the need to backpropagate through a large eddy simulation (LES) solver. Furthermore, a-posteriori methods are challenging to apply broadly since they require significant modification of existing solvers. Finally, both approaches are limited when generalization is desired across different numerical schemes with their implicit filtering characteristics. In this work, we present a deep-learning approach for turbulence closure modeling built on the continuous data assimilation framework. Our approach enables the a-priori training of closures using DNS data observed only at coarse-grid points without modifying or differentiating through the LES solver, while preserving stability during deployment for the recovery of long-term statistics. We focus on the model's ability to adapt to different discretizations by explicitly conditioning it on the numerical scheme. We use two- and three-dimensional canonical cases to test our framework and show that the learned correction systematically tracks the discretization error of the coarse solver.

papers.title: An Annular Spiral Construction for Anomalous Dissipation in the Forced Navier-Stokes Equations
papers.abstract: Kolmogorov's 1941 theory of turbulence (K41) predicts that the rate of kinetic energy dissipation in a turbulent flow can remain positive as viscosity tends to zero. In 2023, Bru\`e and De Lellis used quasi-self-similar mixing to construct solutions of the forced three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations exhibiting anomalous dissipation. In this paper, we show that anomalous dissipation can still occur for a flow with spiral geometry in an annulus. In the horizontal plane, we wind a radial segment into a two-turn spiral and then apply alternating shears. After each pair of shears, the image of the segment shares a subarc of positive length with the original spiral. We compare the vertical velocity with sine profiles whose angular period halves with each pair. After the horizontal flow stops, diffusion damps the final profile. By embedding this planar construction into the $(2+\frac{1}{2})$-dimensional framework, we obtain smooth solutions of the three-dimensional equations with the same smooth initial datum. For a sequence of viscosities tending to zero, their dissipation over a fixed subannulus and one vertical period has a uniform positive lower bound, and their forces converge in $C^\alpha$ uniformly in time for every $0<\alpha<1$. We use this spiral construction to produce solutions of the forced three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations that exhibit anomalous dissipation.

papers.title: An Implicit Discrete Adjoint Unified Gas-Kinetic Scheme for Sensitivity Analysis and Shape Optimization in Multiscale Gas Flows
papers.abstract: Accurate and efficient gradient-based sensitivity evaluation remains challenging for performance optimization in multiscale flows with complex geometries. To address this challenge, this work develops a matrix-free discrete adjoint method for the steady implicit unified gas-kinetic scheme (UGKS) through the exact linearization and transposition of its converged fixed-point operator. The method employs a hybrid differentiation strategy that combines local automatic differentiation (AD) of complex nonlinear kinetic kernels with analytically derived tangent and transpose operators for the coupled macroscopic--microscopic implicit updates and mass-conservation projection. This formulation ensures exact discrete consistency across both flow and geometric dependencies while avoiding global Jacobian assembly and the memory overhead of end-to-end reverse-mode AD. Verification tests across continuum, transitional, and free-molecular regimes confirm machine-precision stepwise duality with the corresponding tangent-linear solver and close agreement with central finite differences. In a six-parameter shape-sensitivity analysis, a single adjoint solve achieves speedups of 7.54X and 3.88X over tangent-linear and central finite-difference evaluations, respectively. Finally, constrained shape optimizations of a periodic Knudsen pump and a Mach-2 NACA0012 airfoil converge within ten design updates, achieving up to 29.68% improvement in normalized mass flow and 7.46% reduction in aerodynamic drag across internal and external multiscale flows.

papers.title: A Steady Theory for Highly Unsteady Thin Airfoil Motions
papers.abstract: A generalized steady thin airfoil theory is built not from steady flow, but from flows in which there exists a frame of reference where the absolute vorticity field is steady. We specialize this general idea to construct a foliation of a domain of phase space for thin airfoil motions in which staying on a leaf of the foliation maintains zero absolute vorticity in the fluid indefinitely. The phase space is described by the airfoil's total rotation rate, speed, and angle of attack. It is found using this definition that one of the preeminent unsteady stall conditions is equivalent to the traditional steady stall condition for this class of flows, various other classical results can be re-interpreted as steady in the absolute vorticity field, and insight is also provided into the surprising experimental results of McGowan et al. (AIAA J. 49, 2011). We show parts of existing quasi-steady flow and Theodorsen unsteady flow theory can be built from a planar approximation of our foliation, making the quasi-steady extension of our theory trivial, and suggesting how an unsteady extension can be created as well. Furthermore, pure unsteady effects in the new theory amount to a transversal of the leaves, occupying just one dimension, inviting interesting prospects for future experimental and theoretical work.

papers.title: Structural and Lagrangian properties of analogue ensembles to characterize multifractality of stochastic processes
papers.abstract: We present a framework for the scale-invariance characterization of stochastic processes in reconstructed finite-dimensional spaces. This framework analyses the structural and dynamical properties of the reconstructed space and is based on a Takens embedding reconstruction followed by the definition of ensembles of analogue states. First, we specify a collection of target states densely sampling the full embedding space. For each target state, we search for the ensemble of its k-nearest neighbors, its k-best analogues, and we analyze its volume and dynamics. On the one hand, we study the probability distribution of the volumes and relate its mean and variance to the scale-invariance properties of the stochastic process. On the second hand, we study the Lagrangian properties of the analogues by characterizing how they disperse in time. More particularly, we study the volume occupied by the analogue's successors in function of time and of their initial volume. The main contribution of this paper is to highlight the link between these dynamical properties and the scale-invariance features of the process. We analyze two types of stationary and dissipative 1-dimensional scale-invariant processes: regularized fractional Brownian motion and regularized multifractal random walk. For both processes, the structure and dynamics of the embedding space are determined by their scale-invariant properties.

papers.title: Resonant lunar tides of Earth's core and basal magma ocean
papers.abstract: Earth's magnetic field is generated by fluid motion in the liquid-metal core and has been active for billions of years. However, prior to the onset of inner-core growth, the sources of mechanical power that drove the geodynamo remain uncertain. During this period, the core may have been overlain by a basal magma ocean (BMO), creating two immiscible fluid layers separated by a density interface, beneath the solid mantle. We develop a theory for lunar tides in this core--BMO system, in which the tidal potential acts on the density contrast between the two layers. The resulting dynamics differ fundamentally from previous models driven by imposed deformation of the core's bounding envelope. In the inviscid limit, the response transitions from an equilibrium tide to an interfacial gravity wave as forcing frequency increases. The two regimes are separated by a resonance that occurs when the forcing frequency matches the natural frequency of the degree-2, order-2 interfacial mode. The inviscid core flow is formally identical to the canonical elliptical vortex, linking the problem to the theory of elliptical instability. Finite viscosity regularises the resonance, introduces phase lag and generates oscillatory boundary layers. Combined with parameterised models of lunar recession and BMO crystallisation, the theory predicts enhanced core-boundary ellipticity, core-flow speed, magnetic Reynolds number and instability metrics, particularly near resonance. These results identify a previously unexplored mechanism for tidally driven flow in differentiated planetary bodies and show that a BMO can enhance tidal coupling to the core, potentially contributing to dynamo action.

papers.title: Construction of a Deployable Closure Model for the Transport of Turbulence Dissipation Rate with Hard-Constrained Physics-Informed Machine Learning
papers.abstract: We present a hard-constrained physics-informed machine learning (PIML) method for constructing a deployable closure model for the transport of turbulence dissipation rate. The framework is built from modules, each performing a single task. The closure module represents the closure with a small network, while the state module represents the flow state during training. The closure network is coupled to the state network through the governing equation residuals. This coupling allows us to learn the closure without using reference closure values as training targets. The coordinate module learns monotone input coordinates that help both networks resolve sharp changes. Within the network architecture, the boundary condition (BC) module imposes boundary values exactly using the Theory of Functional Connections, and the realizability module keeps the closure realizable. We study decaying homogeneous isotropic turbulence (HIT) and learn $\psi$, the closure function governing dissipation rate decay, from trajectories obtained in experiments and direct numerical simulations. Here, the state module is a Deep Operator Network (DeepONet), the BC module imposes the initial state and the closure's low and high Reynolds number limits, and the realizability module ensures growth of the Taylor microscale. The framework reduces the root mean square of the closure variation across ten random seeds by about 95\% relative to the unconstrained model over the training and held-out range. The deployed 18-parameter closure network requires only the Taylor scale Reynolds number $Re_{\lambda_g}$ and can be exported as a standalone C function.

papers.title: Distinguishing photothermal and photoelectrokinetic contributions to flow in light-activated microchannel architectures
papers.abstract: Light-driven flows near Janus surfaces could power microfluidic devices without external hardware. These flows are often attributed to photoinduced electro- or diffusio-osmosis, but illumination also heats the surface, potentially driving natural convection. Here, we map flow and temperature around a UVA-illuminated TiO$_2$-Au Janus membrane using depth-resolved particle tracking and infrared thermometry. Recirculating rolls form on both sides, with no measurable net flow across the membrane. Their cubic, reversing velocity profile identifies horizontal (Hadley) convection, driven by a lateral temperature gradient as the gold film absorbs light. The measured profile agrees with wall-corrected Hadley theory using one fitted parameter. Adding 100 mM NaCl to suppress electrokinetic flows leaves the profile unchanged, indicating that convection dominates. Simulations show that convection falls below 1 $\mu$m/s in thin channels, where surface-driven osmotic flows could dominate. Thus, device geometry and surface chemistry determine which mechanism governs light-driven microfluidic flows.

papers.title: Dynamic Renewal for Hydrodynamic Coupling in Ciliary Mucus Transport
papers.abstract: Mucociliary clearance in large mammalian airways involves millimetric MUC5B-rich mucus strands that emerge from submucosal glands approximately aligned with the direction of transport. These strands are observed downstream in cross-flow networks. Recently, Bos et al. [PNAS Nexus 2, pgad388 (2023)] modeled single strand reorientation using a free-draining coupling for the flow induced by cilia. This leaves unresolved whether the strand's own disturbance of the surrounding liquid assists or frustrates the turning. Here, we develop the methodology to address this question. An immersed-boundary coupling is combined with a Fourier-space Stokes solver and a bespoke dynamic-renewal algorithm that exposes the strand to new ciliary domain without enlarging the simulation volume. This allows us to overcome one of the multiscale challenges posed by mucociliary clearance. We find that hydrodynamic interactions result in only a limited decrease in the rate of reorientation, which supports the use of the free-draining approximation. Future work can build on the methodological foundation introduced here to study collective strand dynamics.

papers.title: Stable eigenmodes of the Large-scale circulation in Turbulent Convection
papers.abstract: Turbulent Rayleigh-B\'enard convection (RBC) is a canonical system for studying buoyancy-driven turbulence. Its defining feature is a system-size large-scale circulation (LSC), whose dynamics reflect the coupling between coherent motion and turbulent fluctuations. Starting from the Boussinesq Navier-Stokes and temperature equations, we derive three coupled stochastic equations for the LSC angular velocity and its associated dipolar temperature field. The deterministic dynamics contain an unstable no-LSC set and two symmetry-related stable finite-LSC states. Linearization about either finite-LSC state yields one purely relaxational eigenmode and a pair of damped oscillatory eigenmodes whose frequency is set by the LSC turnover rate. Turbulent fluctuations continually excite the latter, providing a dynamical origin for the observed quasi-periodic oscillations. Experiments in a thin-disk cell directly resolve both eigenmodes and show their predicted Rayleigh-number scalings. The same stochastic dynamics also provide a route to rare cessations and reversals. This theory-experiment framework provides a tractable example of how coherent circulation states, intrinsic modes, and fluctuation-driven transitions emerge in turbulent convection, with broader relevance to geophysical and astrophysical flows.

papers.title: Coarse-Grained Description of Stochastic Neutron Transport in Highly Heterogeneous Reactor Media via Non-Local Feller Boundary Functionals
papers.abstract: This paper presents a novel hierarchical coarse-graining framework to model non-Markovian neutron transport within the ultra-heterogeneous, multi-phase subcooled nucleate boiling layer of a nuclear reactor core. By applying Feller's subordination theory to continuous-time random walks, microscopic fluid fluctuations and vapor bubble dynamics are rigorously integrated into macroscopic transport operators through the apparatus of Complete Bernstein Functions (CBF). A modified non-local Fick's law is derived using a $P_1$-Legendre polynomial expansion, mapping the fractal porosity and structural phase boundaries into a stochastically renormalized effective diffusion coefficient. The thermodynamic consistency of the model is grounded within Chentsov's statistical manifolds, demonstrating that granular Poisson-like shot noise yields a geometric-exponential family of distributions characterized by a constant negative information curvature. To evaluate operational safety margins under transient conditions, a generalized Lyapunov functional with a quadratic memory kernel is constructed, and a complex decomposition of the transfer function $H(\omega)$ is performed. The resulting analytical limits are parameterized for a WWER-1000 core layout and translated into an engineering computational sequence suitable for implementation in Mathcad Prime 8 to diagnose the onset of Hopf bifurcations and spatial power oscillations.

papers.title: CBTV: Colour Bean Tracking Velocimetry for Dense Granular Flows
papers.abstract: In a dense granular flow, a particle that moves more than about half the spacing between frames is easily confused with a neighbour, and so dense flows are recorded at high frame rates. We present Colour Bean Tracking Velocimetry (CBTV) for particles of a few distinct colours. CBTV first matches small groups of neighbours by position and colour. It then links the remaining particles by relaxation particle tracking velocimetry (PTV) among particles of the same colour, with a search radius set in each frame from the detections. CBTV was compared with ten published trackers on 15 simulated granular flows, with every tracker given the same detections and one global setting. At 2.8 to 13 diameters per frame, on four flows, CBTV keeps 0.595 of the links, against 0.338 for the best published tracker on each cell. It leads that tracker on every cell outside a rotating drum, where every method fails, and trails on none. CBTV was configured on these four flows with their ground truth in view. At steps 1 to 8, on 45 benchmark cases not used in its tuning, CBTV leads the best published tracker on 14 cases and ties on 31, with no deficit. This test is not fully out of sample, because one setting was fixed after a look at part of the benchmark. The ties lie at small displacements. On two unseen flows, a colour-gated relaxation variant built in this work kept more links than CBTV on average. All tests are simulated.

papers.title: A Fitch-Based Wind Farm Parameterization for CM1: Implementation, Validation, and Impacts on Convection Initiation
papers.abstract: We implement a Fitch-based wind farm parameterization in Cloud Model 1 (CM1), representing turbines as elevated momentum sinks and turbulent kinetic energy (TKE) sources within the rotor-swept layer, with optimizations for computational efficiency and parallel execution. Direct comparison with the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model shows close agreement in the magnitude and spatial structure of wind-speed deficits and TKE enhancement. Diurnal simulations also capture the known dependence of boundary layer responses on atmospheric stability, further supporting the consistency of the implementation. Under stable conditions, the wind farm produces coherent spatial patterns in near-surface wind speed and temperature that extend well beyond the farm. In idealized simulations under conditions favorable for convection, large turbines promote convection initiation tens of kilometers downstream, earlier than in the no-farm simulation. Analysis identifies turbulent entrainment of warmer air across the boundary layer top as the dominant source of an elongated downstream warm band, with a smaller contribution from enhanced surface sensible heat flux. Secondary circulations develop across this warm band and provide sustained low-level lifting. A gravity wave generated by the wind farm supplies the initial vertical perturbation, which intensifies as it is advected downstream within an ascending branch of these circulations and develops into a localized deep convective updraft.

papers.title: Fifth-order KdV solitary waves in a nonlinear electrical transmission line
papers.abstract: We report the controlled experimental observation of solitary waves governed by the fifth-order dispersion Korteweg-de Vries (KdV) equation. To achieve vanishing cubic dispersion, we use a mutual inductive coupling between nearest-neighbor inductors within a nonlinear electrical transmission line. We then experimentally characterize the resulting solitary waves through direct spatiotemporal measurements of the dispersion relation, its oscillatory tail profiles, amplitude-width scaling, and amplitude-velocity relation, finding good agreement with semi-analytical predictions. Collision experiments between two (co- or counter-propagating) solitary waves also show that their self-similar profile persists after interaction, up to a time shift. Dissipation effects are also quantified.

papers.title: Fractal dimension of velocity-driven mixing: Reanalysis of Cao et al. (Phys. Rev. A 45, 3841 (1992)) and the universality of the Marstrand co-dimension rule
papers.abstract: Cao et al. [Phys. Rev. A 45, 3841 (1992)] compared box-counting fractal dimensions of interfaces from continuum (SOLA-VOF) and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of zero-Atwood-number mixing driven by random velocity perturbations. They reported D ~ 1.1-1.4 across physical models. We revisit their results with grid-converged geometric VOF simulations and modern box-counting algorithms. The grid-converged continuum dimension depends on the initial-condition realization (D = 1.13-1.38). Independent LAMMPS simulations show that Cao's MD dimension measures thermal scatter of atomic positions, not interface geometry, because their box-counting window lies below the scale of the interface structure: a flat interface at t=0 gives the same D ~ 1.36. When the thermal scatter is filtered by reducing the midpoint cloud to a curve (median binning at 2 sigma), the MD trajectory converges to the same late-time D ~ 1.43 as the continuum, recovering cross-model universality. We prove that the linear-regime box-counting dimension is exactly D = 2 - beta (A > 0) and D = 5/2 - beta (A = 0), where beta is the spectral exponent of the initial perturbation. For white noise (beta = 0) neither formula applies; Cao's early-time D ~ 2 is a boundary artifact. A three-dimensional grid convergence study gives D_3D = 2.361 +/- 0.002 at 400x400x200. Marstrand's co-dimension rule D_3D = D_2D + 1 shows a 7% discrepancy reflecting IC-realization dependence at A = 0, unlike the buoyancy-driven case where the discrepancy falls with resolution.

papers.title: State of Understanding of High-speed Combustion: Can the Detonation Structure in Fuel-Air Mixtures Be Predicted?
papers.abstract: (Abridged) High-speed reacting flows are central to many natural and practical systems, from detonation-based propulsion to various astrophysical phenomena. Here we discuss the limitations in our understanding of high-speed combustion by asking how well modern state-of-the-art physicochemical and computational models can predict the properties of a freely propagating detonation. We present a systematic survey of eleven fuel/air mixtures, from hydrogen, methane, acetylene, and ethylene to JP-10 and n-dodecane jet fuels, at a range of upstream pressures, temperatures, and equivalence ratios. Detonation properties are analyzed using prior numerical studies in the literature, as well as the multi-dimensional, high-fidelity simulations performed in this work, which employ modern multi-step kinetics based on the FFCM/HyChem families of reaction mechanisms. We show that simulations reproduce experimental cell sizes in H$_2$/air at sub-atmospheric pressures or elevated upstream temperatures, yet at the atmospheric conditions, disagreement in the predicted cell sizes is a factor of 3 - 6 at stoichiometric composition and much more severe in lean mixtures. Hydrocarbon fuels show comparable or even larger discrepancies. We argue that such disagreement cannot be ascribed solely to the computational factors, in particular, numerical resolution even at the continuum limit. We analyze the thermodynamic state space occupied by detonations in various mixtures, describe the predicted chemical properties in various regions of the state space, in particular ignition delays and their temperature sensitivity, and consider how well modern chemical kinetics mechanisms are constrained at these conditions by the direct ignition delay measurements. We further assess the proposed role of vibrational non-equilibrium and demonstrate that the current evidence is inconclusive. Finally, we summarize key open questions.

papers.title: Nonpremixed Flames Near the Leading Edge of Parabolic Cylinders
papers.abstract: Nonpremixed flames in the forward stagnation region of porous cylinders are classically described by the first-order stagnation-point boundary layer, which neglects the effects of surface curvature and boundary-layer displacement. In the present work, the description is extended to second order for a porous parabolic cylinder using the method of matched asymptotic expansions. The flame is assumed to be a sheet detached from the porous wall with unity Lewis numbers, and the model accounts for thermal expansion and displacement of the entire reacting layer. The expansion is verified against laminar Navier-Stokes solutions of the same idealized problem, and in the resolved cases the two-term errors decrease approximately as the square of the expansion parameter. At Reynolds numbers typical of laboratory-scale burners, curvature and displacement move the flame away from the wall and reduce the scalar dissipation rate, wall shear, and wall heat flux, whereas the flame temperature changes little. These effects increase with injection, and displacement contributes more over a longer porous section. The second-order terms considerably reduce the errors of the first-order theory in the flame stand-off distance and the scalar dissipation rate.

papers.title: Numerical Study of Flow and Cavitation in Single-Liquid Injectors with Sharp-Edged and Chamfered Orifice Inlets
papers.abstract: In the current work, the investigators used Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) to investigate water flow and cavitation in single-liquid injectors with sharp-edged and chamfered orifice inlets. The k-{\omega} Shear Stress Transport (SST) turbulence model was used along with the Zwart-Gerber-Belamri (ZGB) cavitation model and the Volume of Fluid (VOF) method. The CFD predictions for the volumetric flow rate were validated against existing experimental data for the sharp-edged and chamfered orifice inlets. Pressure drops ranging between 0.07 MPa and 0.59 MPa were considered along with orifice length-to-diameter ratios of 2, 5, and 10. Strong cavitation was observed for the sharp-edged orifice inlet cases with a length-to-diameter ratio of 5 and a pressure drop larger than 0.2 MPa. A hydraulic flip was observed for the sharp-edged orifice inlet with a length-to-diameter ratio of 5 and a pressure drop of 0.59 MPa, which was consistent with the findings from the previous experimental study. Cavitation inception was observed for the chamfered orifice inlet cases with a length-to-diameter ratio of 5 and pressure drops larger than 0.2 MPa. For the sharp-edged orifice inlet with orifice length-to-diameter ratios of 2 and 10, a strong cavitation was observed inside the orifice.

papers.title: A Viscosity-Decoupled Uzawa Lattice Boltzmann Method for Incompressible Flows Across Reynolds Numbers
papers.abstract: Conventional lattice Boltzmann methods (LBMs) tie viscosity to collision relaxation, which induces diffusive stiffness at low Reynolds numbers, non-hydrodynamic instabilities at high Reynolds numbers, and passband breakdown in variable-relaxation dual-time schemes, whereas continuum incompressible solvers require global pressure-Poisson solves every step. We propose a Viscosity-Decoupled Uzawa Lattice Boltzmann Method (VDU-LBM) in D2Q9 and D3Q19 that permanently fixes collision at unit relaxation under smooth harmonic scaling and clears pre-collision non-conserved kinetic memory in one sweep. Constant, heterogeneous, and Smagorinsky eddy viscosities enter through a parameter-free post-streaming bond-symmetric momentum-flux lift that conserves discrete momentum pairwise without perturbing continuity. Variable-step BDF1/BDF2 marching is accelerated by a matrix-free local polynomial Uzawa smoother on the $(d+1)$ conserved moments, paired with link-wise Bouzidi curved walls and shifted ghost open boundaries. Across $\mathrm{Re}\in[10^{-4},10^6]$, VDU-LBM achieves smooth low-Mach second-order space--time accuracy, accelerates unsteady DFG 2D-2 shedding per cycle by $14.27\times\text{--}15.85\times$ over matched 20-core OpenFOAM-v2412, and lowers $256^3$ $\mathrm{Re}=1600$ resolved enstrophy error by $2.25\times$ versus hybrid recursive regularized LBM. On an NVIDIA A100 GPU, the fused D3Q19 solver attains $80.9\%\text{--}85.5\%$ of measured copy bandwidth in multi-pass port traffic and cuts bounded-relaxation diffusive step cost at high viscosity contrasts.

papers.title: How Brine Pockets Evolve and Release in Ice
papers.abstract: Liquid inclusions migrate through solids by melting at one end and freezing at the other, but how a macroscopic phase boundary regulates their deformation and release remains poorly understood. Here, we track individual brine pockets in saline ice through bulk migration, elongation, and release at the ice-water interface, resolving the motion of both ends. In the bulk, temperature-dependent thermomigration gradually elongates the pockets. Near the ice-water interface, the front slows, whereas liquid connection is followed by accelerated rear freezing and rapid shortening. These opposing responses arise from distinct changes in thermal-solutal transport: proximity to the boundary suppresses the local thermal-gradient enhancement and slows front-end melting, while liquid connection enables salt exchange with the surrounding liquid and accelerates rear-end freezing. A quasi-steady diffusion-resistance model captures the dependence of the half-length release time on the pocket length at connection and identifies an effective external exchange length consistent with a salt-balance estimate. Our results identify thermal proximity and liquid connectivity as distinct controls on inclusion evolution and release, providing a framework for understanding liquid redistribution in multicomponent solids.

papers.title: Transient coupling of Marangoni spreading and interfacial waves
papers.abstract: How does an initially non-uniform distribution of surfactant generate waves on a de- formable interface, and how do those waves then govern the redistribution of the surfactant? We answer this question for the linear Cauchy-Poisson problem of an axisymmetric interface between two viscous fluids, released from rest with independently prescribed distributions of surfactant and of interface displacement, by Hankel and Laplace transforms. In Stokes flow the pressure and the viscous normal stress of the Marangoni flow cancel in the nor- mal traction on the interface, for any viscosity ratio, so that the surfactant relaxes without displacing the interface: the coupling between surfactant redistribution and interface de- formation is inertial. With inertia, the Marangoni flow initiates a capillary-gravity wave whose polarity, at leading order for thin boundary layers, is set by the sign of $\rho_l \mu_l - \rho_u \mu_u $, and the surfactant is then carried by the wave, so that its concentration performs weakly damped oscillations at the wave frequency after the Marangoni relaxation of a flat surface has ended. The amplitude of these oscillations is given in closed form at small viscosity; its maximum does not coincide with that of the familiar resonant damping, and the surfactant and the interface shape decouple exactly only when the two fluids have equal densities and viscosities. A localized displacement radiates a wave packet that the surfactant damps, and a localized surfactant redistribution initiates a wave on an initially flat interface. Direct numerical simulations with sharp geometric surfactant transport verify these predictions.

papers.title: AI Meets Turbulence Modeling: Balancing Causation, Correlation, and User Intent
papers.abstract: Turbulence states vary widely in modeling difficulty, requiring distinct paradigms; thus, no single AI or data-driven approach suits all flows. We propose an operational framework classifying data-driven turbulence modeling by balancing physical causation and statistical correlation via non-equilibrium flow memory and user intent. Using the Mori--Zwanzig projection formalism, we decompose unclosed turbulent stress into a local response ($\tau_{ij}^L$) and a spatio-temporally non-local memory integral ($\tau_{ij}^{NL}$). Near statistical equilibrium, rapid relaxation suppresses advective memory, letting local correlations capture physical causation via intrusive $\tau_{ij}^L$ constitutive relations in Reynolds-Averaged Navier--Stokes (RANS) equations. Because the elliptic Poisson equation for fluctuating pressure couples stress evolution to eddy dimensionality beyond single-point velocity-gradient componentiality, local closures are not strictly valid even at equilibrium, yet remain acceptable engineering approximations. In non-equilibrium turbulence, modeling bifurcates by user intent. For predicting unseen geometries, large coherent structures sustain non-local memory ($\tau_{ij}^{NL}$), invalidating local total-stress closures and requiring first-principles causal scale resolution guided by Rules-Augmented AI (RAAI), with resolution set by a recent non-equilibrium theory. Conversely, for rapid design in a known, parameterized coherent flow class, a purely correlational strategy suffices: combining Non-Intrusive Reduced-Order Modeling (NIROM) with uncentered Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) across multi-realization ensembles yields zero-solver synthesis of stationary statistics and unsteady coherent evolution from governing dimensionless parameters. This framework aligns physical causation, statistical correlation, and user intent across flow regimes.
